CHIEF COMPLAINT
Low back pain with right lower extremity paresthesias.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Bryan is a patient who presents with acute onset low back pain and pins and needles sensation in the right foot. Symptoms began yesterday while raking leaves in the yard. Patient felt fine while raking but approximately two hours after returning indoors, he developed tightening of the back and paresthesias in the right foot. Patient reports a similar episode approximately three years ago that resolved within one day. He has tried over-the-counter ibuprofen (two tablets) without relief. Symptoms improve with hot shower and sitting position. Pain is elicited with forward bending but not with extension. Palpation over the L5 area produces tenderness. Denies prolonged physical activity in recent time. Partner notes that pain is particularly worse with standing up from a bent position.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports tingling in right leg. Denies other neurological symptoms. No bowel or bladder dysfunction reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Low back strain approximately three years ago (resolved spontaneously).

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen as needed (recent use without adequate relief).

ALLERGIES
Not documented in this visit.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented in this visit.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient reports low level of physical activity. Lives with partner.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Patient able to ambulate and participate in examination. Lumbar spine: Pain with forward flexion, no pain with extension. Tenderness to palpation at L5. Neurological: Dorsiflexion strength normal bilaterally. Pulses equal in all extremities. Paresthesias noted in right leg.

RESULTS
Lumbosacral spine X-ray: Normal, no acute findings.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Low back strain with right leg paresthesias, likely secondary to acute overexertion from yard work. Plan: (1) Rest and activity modification; (2) Meloxicam prescribed for pain and inflammation; (3) Physical therapy referral to address deconditioning, provide stretching and strengthening exercises; (4) Follow-up in two weeks with phone message to assess progress; (5) MRI of lumbar spine if symptoms persist after two-week trial of conservative management.
